parts.meaning: to stretch forth, point out as a sign

portentous.path: Built on the same root as portend, portentous describes something that stretches forth as an ominous sign, or, ironically, a speaker whose solemnity is puffed up as if every word were an omen.

posit.path: Latin ponere meant to put or place. To posit an idea is to set it down as a starting point for further argument.

parts.meaning: last, last-born (superlative of posterus, coming after)

posthumous.literal: last-born (later reshaped by folk link to 'after burial')
posthumous.path: Latin postumus simply meant 'last,' describing a child born after the father's death. The spelling later shifted to posthumus through false association with humare, to bury, cementing the modern sense of 'after death.'

postulate.path: Latin postulare meant to ask for or demand. To postulate is to demand acceptance of a claim as a starting assumption for an argument.

parts.meaning: powerful, able (from posse, to be able)

potentate.path: Latin potens, able or powerful, gives us potentate, a ruler who wields great power.

powwow.path: Powwow comes from an Algonquian word for a spiritual healer, and the ceremonial gathering held around one. English colonists broadened it to any council or conference, sacred or not.

practice.path: Greek prattein meant to do or act. Practice is literally the doing of something, whether a habitual custom or repeated exercise meant to improve a skill.

practitioner.path: Sharing its root with practice, practitioner names someone who actively does a profession, a doctor, lawyer, or craftsperson, rather than one who only studies it.

parts.meaning: deed, affair, business (from prassein, to do)

pragmatic.path: Greek pragma meant a deed or matter of business. Pragmatic describes an approach grounded in actual deeds and results rather than abstract theory.

prattle.path: Prattle likely echoes the sound of idle chatter itself, an imitative word for talking at length about nothing important.

pre-empt.path: Preemption originally was the legal right to buy land before anyone else got the chance. Pre-empt broadened from buying first to acting first in any way, forestalling someone else's move.

preamble.path: Latin ambulare meant to walk. A preamble 'walks before' the main text, introducing it the way an usher walks ahead of the main party.

precarious.path: Latin precarius described something held only by request or favor, granted at another's pleasure and revocable at any time. That dependency became precarious: unstable because it rests on someone else's whim.

preceded.path: Latin praecedere combined prae, before, and cedere, to go: to go ahead of something else in time or order.

precedent.path: From the same root as precede, a precedent is an earlier case that went before, now used to guide later decisions.

precept.path: Latin praecipere meant to give instruction in advance, literally to 'take beforehand.' A precept is a rule handed down ahead of time to guide conduct.

precipitate.path: Latin praeceps meant headlong, head plunging forward first. To precipitate an event is to throw it headlong into happening, suddenly and abruptly.

precipitous.path: Sharing its root with precipitate, praeceps, headlong, precipitous describes a slope, or a decision, so steep it feels like plunging head-first.

precis.path: Latin praecidere meant to cut off short. A precis is a text cut down to its essential, concise summary.

precision.literal: a cutting off, to an exact point
precision.path: Sharing its root with precise, precision names the quality of being cut exactly to the mark, exact and accurate.

preclude.path: Latin praecludere meant to close something off in advance. To preclude an outcome is to shut the door on it before it can happen.

precocious.path: Latin praecox described fruit that ripened before its season. Precocious borrowed that image for a child whose abilities ripen earlier than expected.

precursor.path: Latin praecursor combined prae, before, with currere, to run: a runner sent ahead. A precursor runs ahead of what follows, a forerunner.

predecessor.path: Latin decedere meant to depart or withdraw. A predecessor is literally the one who stepped down or went away before you took the role.

predicament.path: Praedicamentum was originally a logician's term for a category a thing could be classified under. English narrowed it, oddly, to one specific unwelcome classification: being stuck in a difficult situation.

predilection.path: Latin praediligere meant to love or esteem one thing ahead of others. A predilection is that pre-set favoring, a special liking.

predisposed.path: Latin disponere meant to arrange or set in order. Predisposed adds 'before,' meaning inclined toward something in advance, ahead of any actual event.

preempt.path: Same root as pre-empt: preemption was originally the legal right to buy land before others could. Preempt broadened to acting first in general, before someone else gets the chance.

preemptive.path: From the same root as preempt, preemptive describes an action taken first specifically to forestall someone else's move.

parts.meaning: to trim feathers with the beak

preen.path: Preen's origin is tangled: it may trace to an Old French word for anointing beforehand, or it may simply be a form of 'prune,' to trim. Either way it settled into meaning grooming, literal for a bird, or figurative self-satisfied fussing.

premeditate.path: Latin meditari meant to ponder or think something through. To premeditate is to think a plan through before acting on it.

premise.path: Latin praemittere meant to send ahead. A premise is the proposition sent ahead, put forth first as the foundation the rest of an argument builds on.

prescience.path: Latin praescientia combined prae, before, and scientia, knowledge: knowledge of things before they occur.

prescient.path: Sharing its root with prescience, prescient describes someone who seems to know what is coming before it happens.

presentiment.path: Latin sentire meant to feel or perceive. A presentiment is a feeling that arrives before the event itself, an anticipatory sense that something is coming.

presumption.path: Latin praesumere meant to take something for granted in advance. A presumption is an assumption taken as given, and taking too much for granted without earning it gives the word its other sense, arrogant boldness.

presumptive.path: From the same root as presumption, presumptive describes a conclusion taken as reasonable in advance, based on the evidence at hand rather than proof.

presumptuous.path: Also from praesumere, to take beforehand, presumptuous describes someone who takes for granted a right or familiarity they have not earned, overstepping proper bounds.

pretense.path: Latin praetendere meant to stretch something out in front as a cover or excuse. Pretense is that stretched-forth false front, a show put up to hide the truth.

pretentious.path: From the same root as pretense, pretentious describes someone who stretches their claims to importance further than the truth supports.

preternatural.path: Latin praeter naturam meant literally beyond nature. Preternatural describes something that goes past what is natural, uncanny or almost supernatural.

prevail.path: Latin praevalere meant to have greater strength than others. To prevail is to win out through superior strength, or to become the dominant, widespread state of things.

prevaricate.path: Latin praevaricari originally described a lawyer colluding with the opposing side, literally straddling the issue instead of arguing it straight. Prevaricate kept that sense of dodging the truth by talking around it.

primacy.path: Latin primus meant first. Primacy is simply the state of ranking first in importance.

prime.path: Rooted in primus, first, to prime something, a pump, a canvas, a person, is to put it in its first, ready state before the main action begins.

parts.meaning: first, chief (primus, first + capere, to take)

principled.path: Latin principium meant a foundation or first cause. A principled person acts from firm foundational rules, the 'first things' that guide all their other choices.

pristine.path: Latin pristinus meant belonging to the earliest or former state of things. Pristine kept that sense: something still in its first, unspoiled condition.

probity.path: Latin probus meant genuinely good or upright. Probity is that same tested honesty and integrity of character.

procedural.path: Latin procedere meant to move forward, step by step. Procedural describes anything relating to the fixed steps, the established procedure, by which a process moves forward.

proceeding.path: From the same root as procedural, a proceeding is a formal process that moves forward through set steps, as in a legal or official proceeding.
